# modules.json schema

Field meaning for `<workdir>/crustify/artifacts/modules.json`, the campaign's
decomposition. Layout example: [`templates/modules.json`](../../../templates/modules.json).

Planning emits this repo-tier artifact: the first run creates it, and every run adds what
it lacks and corrects what earlier runs decided, apart from what a frozen module records.
It describes the modules the user's scope selects and every module in their producer
closure.

A module is one translation unit with the headers it defines its items in, as
`decomposition` describes. The decomposition follows the
C codebase rather than a judgement of how it is organized: a module exists because a TU,
or a header that implements what no TU does, exists. It is also the shape the Rust tree
mirrors, as `conventions` describes: there is no second placement document.

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | the analyzed tree's revision — a commit, not a counter. What this decomposition describes, pinned |
| `link_units` | the campaign's link units, in `index` order |

## 1. Indices and order

`index` identifies a link unit, and a module within its link unit; it is not a position.
Each run numbers the link units and modules it adds after the highest index already used,
so an index is never reused or renumbered.

A module's `depends_on` records every dependency it has, as
[Dependencies](#8-link_unitsmodulesdepends_on) describes. The order of the modules is not
recorded here: it is computed from their units' dependencies and recorded in
[`schedule.json`](../schedule-schema/SKILL.md)'s `modules`, with the dependencies it keeps and those it
cuts, as `scheduling`'s Order section describes.

A foundational module depends on foundational modules only, so every foundational module
is ordered before any other, and those whose items depend on others' after them: the
modules of string lifecycle routines after those of the type-erased allocators they call.

## 2. Status

A module's `status` is its decomposition's: `todo` while it may still change, and
`frozen` from the launch of the first batch that homes an item in its file, in its first
wave, of any kind, or in a wrap batch that binds its items ahead of another module's
consumer, or earlier when the user freezes it. A frozen module's decomposition, its
file entries and the homes of its items, and its place in the order, change only when the
user asks: a re-plan neither re-decomposes nor re-homes it, and moves no item into or out
of it. What is derived from the code and the current rules, its `tests`, `depends_on`,
`counters` and `objective`, follows them in every run, frozen or not.

A change of the settings' `campaign` answer, from `wrap` to `port` or back, unfreezes every
module: each is `todo` again, and the next planner run may re-decompose, re-home and
re-order the modules under the new kind. What has landed stays landed: an item whose home
the new decomposition changes keeps its code, which moves to the new home before the next
wave starts.

Freezing a module does not freeze its schedule: its waves that are `todo` may still be
re-planned, and waves appended to it whenever a consumer needs more of it, as
[`schedule-schema`](../schedule-schema/SKILL.md)'s Re-planning section describes. A module's progress is not
recorded here: it is its waves' `status` in `schedule.json`.

## 3. link_units[*]

Each entry's `name` is its identifier; clients may build a name index without losing the
order.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the link unit's id in the campaign, from zero |
| `name` | unique link-unit identifier, normally the linked artifact's filename stem |
| `kind` | `library` or `executable` |
| `linkage` | `shared` or `static` for a library; `null` for an executable |
| `depends_on` | the link units it depends on, by `name` |
| `rust_equivalent` | what Rust already provides in the link unit's place, taken as a whole: `std` and `crates`, as a module's are recorded in [rust_equivalent.std](#61-rust_equivalentstd) and [rust_equivalent.crates](#62-rust_equivalentcrates) |
| `modules` | the link unit's covered modules, in `index` order |

## 4. link_units[*].modules[*]

A module is named by its `name` and `foundational` within its containing link unit: its
globally addressable identity is `(link_unit.name, module.name, module.foundational)`,
written `<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after it for a foundational module.
The name alone suffices but for a split foundational TU, whose two modules share the TU's
path as their name and differ in `foundational`. Every reference to a module, in a
dependency record, a wave or a batch's task, carries both. Its `index` is its permanent
number within the link unit, which orders and numbers the modules a run adds.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the module's id within its link unit, from zero |
| `name` | the path below the C root of its translation unit, or of its header for a header module |
| `status` | `todo` or `frozen`; see [Status](#2-status) |
| `foundational` | `true` for a foundational module, `false` otherwise; see `decomposition`'s Foundational modules section |
| `depends_on` | an array of dependency records; see [Dependencies](#8-link_unitsmodulesdepends_on) |
| `translation_unit` | the module's TU, as a [file entry](#5-file-entries); `null` for a header module |
| `internal_headers` | the headers the build does not install that the module defines items in, as file entries |
| `api_headers` | the headers the build installs that the module defines or declares items in, as file entries |
| `tests` | the test files tied to the module, those whose subject it is, as file entries whose `items` select test functions; see [File entries](#5-file-entries) |
| `objective` | the translation intent recorded for this module |
| `counters` | what the module contains |

A header module, one with a `null` `translation_unit`, holds a header that implements what
no TU does, such as `static inline` functions or globals of its own, and lists it in
`internal_headers` or `api_headers` as the build installs it or not.

## 5. File entries

Every file a module lists is an entry:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | the file's path below the C root |
| `items` | `included` and `excluded`, each an array of the C entity names the file defines or declares |

With both lists empty, the module owns every entity the file defines or declares. With
`included`, it owns only those; with `excluded`, every other one. A file entry sets one
list at most. A typedef follows the type it names, so naming a struct or its typedef
selects both. A macro is owned as any entity is when it is API, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.

Every entity is owned by exactly one module, and every translation unit is listed by
exactly one module, apart from a foundational split, whose two modules list it with the
same names, one as `included` and the other as `excluded`. A header may be listed by
several modules, each owning the entities its lists select: the module bundled with the
header usually owns it whole, or with `excluded` the entities other modules take, and each
of those lists it with them as `included`.

The owner counts, homes and translates an entity; every other module reaches it through
an ordinary dependency record.

Test files are not owned: a test file is listed in the `tests` of every module it is
tied to, as `decomposition`'s Bundling section describes, and its entry's
`items` name the test functions tied to that module, empty when the whole file is.

## 6. link_units[*].modules[*].objective

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `objective` | `wrap` to preserve the C implementation behind a safe Rust API, or `port` to reimplement it in safe Rust |
| `rust_equivalent` | what Rust already provides in its place: `std` and `crates`, below |

A module carries one objective, which the settings' `campaign` answer sets, as
`decomposition`'s Objectives section describes: `port` in a port
campaign and `wrap` in a wrap campaign, and `wrap` for every foundational module in either.
A TU is not split for its objective.

### 6.1 rust_equivalent.std

The closest the Rust standard library (`core`, `alloc` and `std`) comes to providing the
module in its place, taken as a whole: every item it owns. `null` when the standard
library provides none of it.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `library` | the standard-library paths that come closest to providing it, modules or types such as `alloc::vec::Vec` or `core::str` |
| `feature_parity` | `full` when replacing the module with them gains exactly the module's functionality, `partial` otherwise |
| `notes` | for `partial`, what is missing or differs; empty for `full` |

### 6.2 rust_equivalent.crates

Established crates that could replace the module outright, in descending order of
feature parity; empty when none applies.

| `crates[*]` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `crate` | the crate's name on crates.io |
| `feature_parity` | `full` or `partial`, as for `std` |
| `license` | its SPDX license expression |
| `notes` | what is missing or differs: semantics, platform support or performance; empty when nothing |

Each candidate is checked for its semantics, platform support, performance and licensing
before it is listed.

A crate that reimplements or binds the target itself, the repository or one of its link
units, is not listed, nor is one of its components: replacing the target is what the
campaign does, so such a crate is no equivalent of a module or a link unit but an
alternative to the campaign. A general-purpose crate that also serves such a
reimplementation is listed on its own merits.

## 7. link_units[*].modules[*].counters

Two blocks with the same fields: `implementation` counts what the module's
`translation_unit` and `internal_headers` define, and `api` counts what its `api_headers`
publish. Only entities the module owns are counted, so a shared header's entities count
once across the decomposition.

| `implementation` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `files` | number of file entries in `translation_unit` and `internal_headers` |
| `loc` | physical nonblank, noncomment lines across the entities it owns |
| `structs` | struct definitions |
| `functions` | function definitions |
| `global_variables` | file- and program-scope variables |
| `unions` | union definitions |
| `function_pointers` | function pointers the module defines, declared by a typedef or written inline |

| `api` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `files` | number of entries in `api_headers` |
| `loc` | physical nonblank, noncomment lines across the entities it owns |
| `structs` | structs whose body the API headers publish |
| `opaque_structs` | structs the API headers only forward-declare |
| `functions` | functions the API headers declare, prototypes and `static inline` alike |
| `global_variables` | variables the API headers declare |
| `unions` | unions the API headers define |
| `function_pointers` | function pointers the API headers define, declared by a typedef or written inline |

The blocks overlap: a function defined in a translation unit and declared in an API
header counts in both, once as a definition and once as published. Never add them.

Enums, macros and typedefs of their own are not counted yet, here or in a dependency
record.
<!-- TODO: count them, as the wavefront skill's TODO says. -->

## 8. link_units[*].modules[*].depends_on

Every record is directed from this module, the consumer, to something it depends on: a
module of the decomposition, or an out-of-tree library, which depends on none of the
modules and so forms no cycle with them. Which in-tree dependencies the order keeps and
which it cuts is `schedule.json`'s. Imported producer modules are emitted as modules too,
so every in-tree record resolves through `link_units`.

| in-tree record field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `link_unit` | destination `link_units[*].name` |
| `module` | destination module's `name` within that link unit |
| `foundational` | the destination module's `foundational`, which tells the two modules of a split TU apart |
| `outgoing_edges` | dependency edges from this module to the destination |
| `incoming_edges` | dependency edges from the destination back to this module |
| `counters` | distinct entities consumed from that destination, by kind |

`outgoing_edges` is what this module needs from the destination; `incoming_edges` is what
the destination needs from it, and is non-zero exactly when the two form a cycle. The pair
is mirrored: the destination's own record for this module, when the two form a cycle,
carries the same two numbers swapped.

| out-of-tree record field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `library` | external library depended on, as linked: a `libraries[*].name` of `dependencies.json` |
| `counters` | distinct entities consumed from it, by kind |

What the campaign knows of the library itself, the release the target links, its source,
its wrapper and the crates that port or bind it, is recorded once, in `dependencies.json`,
as `dependencies-schema` describes, not in each record that imports it.

A record's `counters` carries the same item kinds a module's own does — `structs`,
`functions`, `global_variables`, `unions`, `function_pointers` — counting what this module
consumes, not what the destination contains. A module that uses only another's enums has
no record of it yet, and its edges count no enum. It has no `files` or `loc`: those
describe a module's own files, and a consumer imports entities, not files.

The in-tree graph may contain cycles, and these records keep them: a record whose
`incoming_edges` is non-zero is one side of a cycle, which the order cuts.

# schedule.json schema

Field meaning for `<workdir>/crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, the campaign's module
order, waves and batches. Layout examples: [`templates/schedule.json`](../../../templates/schedule.json), and a port
campaign's, [`templates/schedule.port.json`](../../../templates/schedule.port.json).

The campaign has one schedule, which every planner run extends: the first run creates it,
and each later one appends the waves its scope adds and re-plans the waves that have not
started. Waves are computable in advance, so writing them down makes a campaign's shape
reviewable before it spends anything; their batches are not, since they are packed when
each wave starts, as `scheduling`'s Batches section describes.

An audit's review waves are not recorded in it.

The schedule holds two kinds of field:

- the plan: the order of the modules, the waves, their dependencies and their items,
  decided by planning; and
- the progress: each wave's `status` and `packed_with`, and its `batches`, each with its
  worklist, `status` and `commits`, recorded as the work launches and lands.

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `6` |
| `modules` | the order of the campaign's modules, one record per module the schedule holds waves of, by `layer` |
| `waves` | the campaign's waves, in `index` order |

## 1. modules[*]

The order of the modules is computed over every module of the decomposition, as
`scheduling`'s Order section describes, and recorded here, with the
dependencies it keeps and those it cuts.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the module's identity in `modules.json`, as its `link_units[*].name`, its `name` and its `foundational` |
| `layer` | its place in the order of the modules: 0 for one that depends on no module ordered before it, else one more than the highest of those it depends on |
| `waves` | the indices of its waves |
| `depends_on.scheduled` | the modules it depends on that are ordered before it, each a dependency record below |
| `depends_on.cut` | the modules it depends on that are ordered after it, its dependency on them cut to break a cycle, each a dependency record with its `items` |
| `depends_on.external` | the out-of-tree libraries its units use, each an out-of-tree record below |

A dependency record names the module depended on, by `link_unit`, `module` and
`foundational`, and counts what this module's units use of it:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `unique_edges` | the distinct units of that module they use: one binding each, when the dependency is cut |
| `total_edges` | every unit edge from this module's units to that module's |
| `items` | on a cut record: each edge it cuts, as `from` (this module's unit), `to` (the other module's unit), each `{name, defined_in}`, and the `kind` of `to`, as an item's |

An out-of-tree record names the library its units use, by its `library`, a
`libraries[*].name` of `dependencies.json`, and counts what they use of it, with the
`unique_edges` and `total_edges` of a dependency record and every edge in its `items`, as
on a cut record: `to` is the library's entity, by the name and the defining header its
users reference. No entity of the library is a unit of this schedule: its side campaign
wraps it, before the first wave that holds a `from` of the record, as
`dependencies`'s Side campaigns section describes.

`scheduled` alone is acyclic across the schedule, and with `cut` it is every module this
one depends on. A planner run rewrites `modules` from its order; the waves that have
started keep their records, as [Re-planning](#5-re-planning) describes.

## 2. waves[*]

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the wave's id, from zero; see [Indices](#4-indices) |
| `link_unit` | the `link_units[*].name` of `modules.json` its units belong to |
| `module` | the module's `name` within that link unit |
| `foundational` | the module's `foundational` |
| `layer` | its module's `layer`; `null` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `sublayer` | its place among its module's waves, from 0; `null` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `status` | `todo`, `wip` or `done` |
| `depends_on` | the waves this one depends on: `scheduled` and `cut`, each an array of wave indices |
| `items` | the wave's items, each a planned item below |
| `packed_with` | the index of the earlier wave whose batches hold this wave's items, when the two share batches; `null` otherwise |
| `batches` | the wave's batches, which execute in parallel; empty until the wave starts |

A planned item is a batch item, as `task-schema` describes its `items`, with
the objective it is translated with and its entity's release points:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `defined_in`, `kind`, `field_users`, `typedefs`, `home` | as on a batch item |
| `objective` | `wrap` or `port`, or one of the later stages of `scheduling`'s Later stages section: `port/layout` or `port/memory` for a struct or a union, `port/layout` for a closed enum, `port/unexport` for a function, a global or a function pointer |
| `opaque_after` | on a struct, a union or an enum, the release point after which none of its layout users is left, as the scheduling spec's Later stages section defines them; `null` on any other item |
| `memory_unmanaged_after` | on a struct or a union, the release point after which none of its memory users is left; `null` on any other item |
| `unreferenced_after` | on a function, a global, a macro, a function pointer or a typedef, the release point after which none of its referrers is left, and for a function pointer written inline none of what reaches the sites that write it; `null` on any other item |
| `carries_over` | on a `port/unexport` item, the C test cases and harness code still referencing its export when its wave runs, in the plan's order, below; absent on every other objective |

A release point has two records, `closure` over every user and `scheduled` over those the
schedule holds, each naming the last users, their waves and their `modules`, as the
planning tools compute them. An entity's planned items carry the same release points. The
wave of a later stage lists, among its `depends_on.scheduled`, the last wave of each module
its release point's `closure.modules` names but the item's own, so that it runs once those
modules have switched: `opaque_after` for `port/layout`, `memory_unmanaged_after` for
`port/memory`, and `unreferenced_after` for `port/unexport`.

A `port/unexport` item's `carries_over` records what of the target's C tests its stage
carries over and removes from `c/`, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes:

| `carries_over` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `cases` | the test cases still referencing the export when the wave runs, each `{path, tests}`: the test file and its test case names |
| `if_still_in_c` | the cases, shaped as `cases`, that reference the export but that the plan's order removes before the wave, by a module's switch or another wave's carry-over it does not depend on: the stage carries over those still in `c/` when it runs |
| `harness` | the functions of the test harness, as `file:function`, that reference the export, which the stage adapts |

The plan's order on disk decides which wave carries over a case several of them
reference: the first by index that runs after the case's last chance to leave otherwise.
A wave whose dependencies let it run earlier carries over what is still in `c/` when it
runs, which its batch checks against the record.

`depends_on.scheduled` lists the waves that complete before this one: its module's
previous wave, and the waves that hold its items' dependencies. `depends_on.cut` lists the
waves that hold its items' cut dependencies, which run after it; it reaches what they hold
through the safe wrappers a wrap batch before it adds, as `scheduling`'s
Wrap batches section describes. Their union is every wave this one depends on, and
`scheduled` alone is acyclic across the schedule.

Every wave belongs to one module, as `scheduling` describes.

A wave is `todo` until its first batch launches, `wip` while any of its batches is
running or has failed, and `done` once every batch has landed and the wave has been
promoted. A wave `packed_with` another has no batches of its own: its `status` follows
that wave's, and it lands on that wave's integration branch.

## 3. waves[*].batches[*]

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the batch's id within its wave, from zero |
| `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the module whose units it holds, as for its wave; `null`, `null` and `false` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `kind` | an objective of its items, as a planned item's, or `review` |
| `status` | `todo`, `wip`, `done` or `failed` |
| `items` | a translation batch's worklist, as `task-schema` describes its `items` |
| `reviews` | a `review` batch's worklist: the indices of the batches of its wave it reviews; empty in a module pass |
| `module_pass` | optional, `false` when absent: `true` on the `review` batch that reviews its module whole, the last batch of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items, as `reviewing`'s Review batches section describes |
| `commits` | the commits the batch landed, in order; empty until it lands |

The batches are packed when the wave starts, and added as it runs: a batch that fails may
be packed again into new batches, which take the next free indices, and review batches are
added as the batches they review land, as `reviewing` describes. A
batch's items are those of its wave, of the waves `packed_with` it, or, in a wrap batch
that binds what its consumers need ahead of them, items of other modules, which keep
their homes there, as `scheduling`'s Wrap batches section describes.
Its `link_unit`, `module` and `foundational` are always its wave's.

A batch is `todo` until its agent launches, `wip` while an agent runs it, `done` once it
has landed every item of its worklist, and `failed` when its last agent ended without
landing. An item's status is that of the batch that holds it: a planned item is translated
once a batch holding it with its objective is `done`.

A batch's `commits` are its landing's commits as they sit on its wave branch, which a
promotion fast-forwards without rewriting them.

## 4. Indices

A started wave's `index` is its permanent id: its branch, the batch ids
`wave-<index>/batch-<index>` and the run dirs are named from it, so it is never reused,
renumbered or moved, and they keep identifying the same work.

A `todo` wave's index names nothing yet. Each planner run numbers the `todo` waves after
the highest index of a started wave, from the next integer, in one topological order of
their `depends_on.scheduled`, with no gaps, renumbering their `depends_on` with them. The
indices of the `todo` waves are therefore their order: the plan is one total order on
disk, which the waves follow as they start, as many at once as their dependencies and the
host allow, and which folding waves into shared batches when they start, as
`scheduling`'s Batches section describes, leaves as it is.

## 5. Re-planning

Only waves that are `todo` are re-planned: a re-plan may change, split or remove them,
and the waves that replace them are numbered with the other `todo` waves, as
[Indices](#4-indices) describes. A wave that is `wip` or `done` keeps
its record, apart from the progress fields, and is never revisited, and its items are not
scheduled again. An item a batch has landed with its objective, such as one bound ahead of
its consumer, is not scheduled again with that objective. A frozen module's waves that are
`todo` are re-planned like any other, within its frozen decomposition, and waves may be
appended to it, such as those a module added after it calls for. A change of the
settings' `campaign` answer unfreezes every module, as `modules-schema`'s
Status section describes, and every `todo` wave is re-planned under the new kind.

## 6. Derived paths

A batch's id, `wave-<index>/batch-<index>`, names its branch and worktree, and its wave
index the wave branch, as `versioning` spells them, and with its module its run dirs and
reviews dir, as `layout` spells them, each run's `task.json` naming the batch's wave and
index.

## 3. link_units[*]

Each entry's `name` is its identifier; clients may build a name index without losing the
order.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the link unit's id in the campaign, from zero |
| `name` | unique link-unit identifier, normally the linked artifact's filename stem |
| `kind` | `library` or `executable` |
| `linkage` | `shared` or `static` for a library; `null` for an executable |
| `depends_on` | the link units it depends on, by `name` |
| `rust_equivalent` | what Rust already provides in the link unit's place, taken as a whole: `std` and `crates`, as a module's are recorded in [rust_equivalent.std](#61-rust_equivalentstd) and [rust_equivalent.crates](#62-rust_equivalentcrates) |
| `modules` | the link unit's covered modules, in `index` order |

## 4. link_units[*].modules[*]

A module is named by its `name` and `foundational` within its containing link unit: its
globally addressable identity is `(link_unit.name, module.name, module.foundational)`,
written `<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after it for a foundational module.
The name alone suffices but for a split foundational TU, whose two modules share the TU's
path as their name and differ in `foundational`. Every reference to a module, in a
dependency record, a wave or a batch's task, carries both. Its `index` is its permanent
number within the link unit, which orders and numbers the modules a run adds.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the module's id within its link unit, from zero |
| `name` | the path below the C root of its translation unit, or of its header for a header module |
| `status` | `todo` or `frozen`; see [Status](#2-status) |
| `foundational` | `true` for a foundational module, `false` otherwise; see `decomposition`'s Foundational modules section |
| `depends_on` | an array of dependency records; see [Dependencies](#8-link_unitsmodulesdepends_on) |
| `translation_unit` | the module's TU, as a [file entry](#5-file-entries); `null` for a header module |
| `internal_headers` | the headers the build does not install that the module defines items in, as file entries |
| `api_headers` | the headers the build installs that the module defines or declares items in, as file entries |
| `tests` | the test files tied to the module, those whose subject it is, as file entries whose `items` select test functions; see [File entries](#5-file-entries) |
| `objective` | the translation intent recorded for this module |
| `counters` | what the module contains |

A header module, one with a `null` `translation_unit`, holds a header that implements what
no TU does, such as `static inline` functions or globals of its own, and lists it in
`internal_headers` or `api_headers` as the build installs it or not.

## 5. File entries

Every file a module lists is an entry:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | the file's path below the C root |
| `items` | `included` and `excluded`, each an array of the C entity names the file defines or declares |

With both lists empty, the module owns every entity the file defines or declares. With
`included`, it owns only those; with `excluded`, every other one. A file entry sets one
list at most. A typedef follows the type it names, so naming a struct or its typedef
selects both. A macro is owned as any entity is when it is API, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.

Every entity is owned by exactly one module, and every translation unit is listed by
exactly one module, apart from a foundational split, whose two modules list it with the
same names, one as `included` and the other as `excluded`. A header may be listed by
several modules, each owning the entities its lists select: the module bundled with the
header usually owns it whole, or with `excluded` the entities other modules take, and each
of those lists it with them as `included`.

The owner counts, homes and translates an entity; every other module reaches it through
an ordinary dependency record.

Test files are not owned: a test file is listed in the `tests` of every module it is
tied to, as `decomposition`'s Bundling section describes, and its entry's
`items` name the test functions tied to that module, empty when the whole file is.

## 6. link_units[*].modules[*].objective

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `objective` | `wrap` to preserve the C implementation behind a safe Rust API, or `port` to reimplement it in safe Rust |
| `rust_equivalent` | what Rust already provides in its place: `std` and `crates`, below |

A module carries one objective, which the settings' `campaign` answer sets, as
`decomposition`'s Objectives section describes: `port` in a port
campaign and `wrap` in a wrap campaign, and `wrap` for every foundational module in either.
A TU is not split for its objective.

### 6.1 rust_equivalent.std

The closest the Rust standard library (`core`, `alloc` and `std`) comes to providing the
module in its place, taken as a whole: every item it owns. `null` when the standard
library provides none of it.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `library` | the standard-library paths that come closest to providing it, modules or types such as `alloc::vec::Vec` or `core::str` |
| `feature_parity` | `full` when replacing the module with them gains exactly the module's functionality, `partial` otherwise |
| `notes` | for `partial`, what is missing or differs; empty for `full` |

### 6.2 rust_equivalent.crates

Established crates that could replace the module outright, in descending order of
feature parity; empty when none applies.

| `crates[*]` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `crate` | the crate's name on crates.io |
| `feature_parity` | `full` or `partial`, as for `std` |
| `license` | its SPDX license expression |
| `notes` | what is missing or differs: semantics, platform support or performance; empty when nothing |

Each candidate is checked for its semantics, platform support, performance and licensing
before it is listed.

A crate that reimplements or binds the target itself, the repository or one of its link
units, is not listed, nor is one of its components: replacing the target is what the
campaign does, so such a crate is no equivalent of a module or a link unit but an
alternative to the campaign. A general-purpose crate that also serves such a
reimplementation is listed on its own merits.

## 7. link_units[*].modules[*].counters

Two blocks with the same fields: `implementation` counts what the module's
`translation_unit` and `internal_headers` define, and `api` counts what its `api_headers`
publish. Only entities the module owns are counted, so a shared header's entities count
once across the decomposition.

| `implementation` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `files` | number of file entries in `translation_unit` and `internal_headers` |
| `loc` | physical nonblank, noncomment lines across the entities it owns |
| `structs` | struct definitions |
| `functions` | function definitions |
| `global_variables` | file- and program-scope variables |
| `unions` | union definitions |
| `function_pointers` | function pointers the module defines, declared by a typedef or written inline |

| `api` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `files` | number of entries in `api_headers` |
| `loc` | physical nonblank, noncomment lines across the entities it owns |
| `structs` | structs whose body the API headers publish |
| `opaque_structs` | structs the API headers only forward-declare |
| `functions` | functions the API headers declare, prototypes and `static inline` alike |
| `global_variables` | variables the API headers declare |
| `unions` | unions the API headers define |
| `function_pointers` | function pointers the API headers define, declared by a typedef or written inline |

The blocks overlap: a function defined in a translation unit and declared in an API
header counts in both, once as a definition and once as published. Never add them.

Enums, macros and typedefs of their own are not counted yet, here or in a dependency
record.
<!-- TODO: count them, as the wavefront skill's TODO says. -->

## 8. link_units[*].modules[*].depends_on

Every record is directed from this module, the consumer, to something it depends on: a
module of the decomposition, or an out-of-tree library, which depends on none of the
modules and so forms no cycle with them. Which in-tree dependencies the order keeps and
which it cuts is `schedule.json`'s. Imported producer modules are emitted as modules too,
so every in-tree record resolves through `link_units`.

| in-tree record field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `link_unit` | destination `link_units[*].name` |
| `module` | destination module's `name` within that link unit |
| `foundational` | the destination module's `foundational`, which tells the two modules of a split TU apart |
| `outgoing_edges` | dependency edges from this module to the destination |
| `incoming_edges` | dependency edges from the destination back to this module |
| `counters` | distinct entities consumed from that destination, by kind |

`outgoing_edges` is what this module needs from the destination; `incoming_edges` is what
the destination needs from it, and is non-zero exactly when the two form a cycle. The pair
is mirrored: the destination's own record for this module, when the two form a cycle,
carries the same two numbers swapped.

| out-of-tree record field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `library` | external library depended on, as linked: a `libraries[*].name` of `dependencies.json` |
| `counters` | distinct entities consumed from it, by kind |

What the campaign knows of the library itself, the release the target links, its source,
its wrapper and the crates that port or bind it, is recorded once, in `dependencies.json`,
as `dependencies-schema` describes, not in each record that imports it.

A record's `counters` carries the same item kinds a module's own does — `structs`,
`functions`, `global_variables`, `unions`, `function_pointers` — counting what this module
consumes, not what the destination contains. A module that uses only another's enums has
no record of it yet, and its edges count no enum. It has no `files` or `loc`: those
describe a module's own files, and a consumer imports entities, not files.

The in-tree graph may contain cycles, and these records keep them: a record whose
`incoming_edges` is non-zero is one side of a cycle, which the order cuts.

description: "The fields of schedule.json: modules, waves, items, batches, progress, indices and re-planning. Read before writing or reading schedule.json."

# schedule.json schema

Field meaning for `<workdir>/crustify/artifacts/schedule.json`, the campaign's module
order, waves and batches. Layout examples: [`templates/schedule.json`](../../../templates/schedule.json), and a port
campaign's, [`templates/schedule.port.json`](../../../templates/schedule.port.json).

The campaign has one schedule, which every planner run extends: the first run creates it,
and each later one appends the waves its scope adds and re-plans the waves that have not
started. Waves are computable in advance, so writing them down makes a campaign's shape
reviewable before it spends anything; their batches are not, since they are packed when
each wave starts, as `scheduling`'s Batches section describes.

An audit's review waves are not recorded in it.

The schedule holds two kinds of field:

- the plan: the order of the modules, the waves, their dependencies and their items,
  decided by planning; and
- the progress: each wave's `status` and `packed_with`, and its `batches`, each with its
  worklist, `status` and `commits`, recorded as the work launches and lands.

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `6` |
| `modules` | the order of the campaign's modules, one record per module the schedule holds waves of, by `layer` |
| `waves` | the campaign's waves, in `index` order |

## 1. modules[*]

The order of the modules is computed over every module of the decomposition, as
`scheduling`'s Order section describes, and recorded here, with the
dependencies it keeps and those it cuts.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the module's identity in `modules.json`, as its `link_units[*].name`, its `name` and its `foundational` |
| `layer` | its place in the order of the modules: 0 for one that depends on no module ordered before it, else one more than the highest of those it depends on |
| `waves` | the indices of its waves |
| `depends_on.scheduled` | the modules it depends on that are ordered before it, each a dependency record below |
| `depends_on.cut` | the modules it depends on that are ordered after it, its dependency on them cut to break a cycle, each a dependency record with its `items` |
| `depends_on.external` | the out-of-tree libraries its units use, each an out-of-tree record below |

A dependency record names the module depended on, by `link_unit`, `module` and
`foundational`, and counts what this module's units use of it:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `unique_edges` | the distinct units of that module they use: one binding each, when the dependency is cut |
| `total_edges` | every unit edge from this module's units to that module's |
| `items` | on a cut record: each edge it cuts, as `from` (this module's unit), `to` (the other module's unit), each `{name, defined_in}`, and the `kind` of `to`, as an item's |

An out-of-tree record names the library its units use, by its `library`, a
`libraries[*].name` of `dependencies.json`, and counts what they use of it, with the
`unique_edges` and `total_edges` of a dependency record and every edge in its `items`, as
on a cut record: `to` is the library's entity, by the name and the defining header its
users reference. No entity of the library is a unit of this schedule: its side campaign
wraps it, before the first wave that holds a `from` of the record, as
`dependencies`'s Side campaigns section describes.

`scheduled` alone is acyclic across the schedule, and with `cut` it is every module this
one depends on. A planner run rewrites `modules` from its order; the waves that have
started keep their records, as [Re-planning](#5-re-planning) describes.

## 2. waves[*]

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the wave's id, from zero; see [Indices](#4-indices) |
| `link_unit` | the `link_units[*].name` of `modules.json` its units belong to |
| `module` | the module's `name` within that link unit |
| `foundational` | the module's `foundational` |
| `layer` | its module's `layer`; `null` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `sublayer` | its place among its module's waves, from 0; `null` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `status` | `todo`, `wip` or `done` |
| `depends_on` | the waves this one depends on: `scheduled` and `cut`, each an array of wave indices |
| `items` | the wave's items, each a planned item below |
| `packed_with` | the index of the earlier wave whose batches hold this wave's items, when the two share batches; `null` otherwise |
| `batches` | the wave's batches, which execute in parallel; empty until the wave starts |

A planned item is a batch item, as `task-schema` describes its `items`, with
the objective it is translated with and its entity's release points:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `defined_in`, `kind`, `field_users`, `typedefs`, `home` | as on a batch item |
| `objective` | `wrap` or `port`, or one of the later stages of `scheduling`'s Later stages section: `port/layout` or `port/memory` for a struct or a union, `port/layout` for a closed enum, `port/unexport` for a function, a global or a function pointer |
| `opaque_after` | on a struct, a union or an enum, the release point after which none of its layout users is left, as the scheduling spec's Later stages section defines them; `null` on any other item |
| `memory_unmanaged_after` | on a struct or a union, the release point after which none of its memory users is left; `null` on any other item |
| `unreferenced_after` | on a function, a global, a macro, a function pointer or a typedef, the release point after which none of its referrers is left, and for a function pointer written inline none of what reaches the sites that write it; `null` on any other item |
| `carries_over` | on a `port/unexport` item, the C test cases and harness code still referencing its export when its wave runs, in the plan's order, below; absent on every other objective |

A release point has two records, `closure` over every user and `scheduled` over those the
schedule holds, each naming the last users, their waves and their `modules`, as the
planning tools compute them. An entity's planned items carry the same release points. The
wave of a later stage lists, among its `depends_on.scheduled`, the last wave of each module
its release point's `closure.modules` names but the item's own, so that it runs once those
modules have switched: `opaque_after` for `port/layout`, `memory_unmanaged_after` for
`port/memory`, and `unreferenced_after` for `port/unexport`.

A `port/unexport` item's `carries_over` records what of the target's C tests its stage
carries over and removes from `c/`, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes:

| `carries_over` field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `cases` | the test cases still referencing the export when the wave runs, each `{path, tests}`: the test file and its test case names |
| `if_still_in_c` | the cases, shaped as `cases`, that reference the export but that the plan's order removes before the wave, by a module's switch or another wave's carry-over it does not depend on: the stage carries over those still in `c/` when it runs |
| `harness` | the functions of the test harness, as `file:function`, that reference the export, which the stage adapts |

The plan's order on disk decides which wave carries over a case several of them
reference: the first by index that runs after the case's last chance to leave otherwise.
A wave whose dependencies let it run earlier carries over what is still in `c/` when it
runs, which its batch checks against the record.

`depends_on.scheduled` lists the waves that complete before this one: its module's
previous wave, and the waves that hold its items' dependencies. `depends_on.cut` lists the
waves that hold its items' cut dependencies, which run after it; it reaches what they hold
through the safe wrappers a wrap batch before it adds, as `scheduling`'s
Wrap batches section describes. Their union is every wave this one depends on, and
`scheduled` alone is acyclic across the schedule.

Every wave belongs to one module, as `scheduling` describes.

A wave is `todo` until its first batch launches, `wip` while any of its batches is
running or has failed, and `done` once every batch has landed and the wave has been
promoted. A wave `packed_with` another has no batches of its own: its `status` follows
that wave's, and it lands on that wave's integration branch.

## 3. waves[*].batches[*]

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `index` | the batch's id within its wave, from zero |
| `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the module whose units it holds, as for its wave; `null`, `null` and `false` when the campaign has no decomposition |
| `kind` | an objective of its items, as a planned item's, or `review` |
| `status` | `todo`, `wip`, `done` or `failed` |
| `items` | a translation batch's worklist, as `task-schema` describes its `items` |
| `reviews` | a `review` batch's worklist: the indices of the batches of its wave it reviews; empty in a module pass |
| `module_pass` | optional, `false` when absent: `true` on the `review` batch that reviews its module whole, the last batch of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items, as `reviewing`'s Review batches section describes |
| `commits` | the commits the batch landed, in order; empty until it lands |

The batches are packed when the wave starts, and added as it runs: a batch that fails may
be packed again into new batches, which take the next free indices, and review batches are
added as the batches they review land, as `reviewing` describes. A
batch's items are those of its wave, of the waves `packed_with` it, or, in a wrap batch
that binds what its consumers need ahead of them, items of other modules, which keep
their homes there, as `scheduling`'s Wrap batches section describes.
Its `link_unit`, `module` and `foundational` are always its wave's.

A batch is `todo` until its agent launches, `wip` while an agent runs it, `done` once it
has landed every item of its worklist, and `failed` when its last agent ended without
landing. An item's status is that of the batch that holds it: a planned item is translated
once a batch holding it with its objective is `done`.

A batch's `commits` are its landing's commits as they sit on its wave branch, which a
promotion fast-forwards without rewriting them.

## 4. Indices

A started wave's `index` is its permanent id: its branch, the batch ids
`wave-<index>/batch-<index>` and the run dirs are named from it, so it is never reused,
renumbered or moved, and they keep identifying the same work.

A `todo` wave's index names nothing yet. Each planner run numbers the `todo` waves after
the highest index of a started wave, from the next integer, in one topological order of
their `depends_on.scheduled`, with no gaps, renumbering their `depends_on` with them. The
indices of the `todo` waves are therefore their order: the plan is one total order on
disk, which the waves follow as they start, as many at once as their dependencies and the
host allow, and which folding waves into shared batches when they start, as
`scheduling`'s Batches section describes, leaves as it is.

## 5. Re-planning

Only waves that are `todo` are re-planned: a re-plan may change, split or remove them,
and the waves that replace them are numbered with the other `todo` waves, as
[Indices](#4-indices) describes. A wave that is `wip` or `done` keeps
its record, apart from the progress fields, and is never revisited, and its items are not
scheduled again. An item a batch has landed with its objective, such as one bound ahead of
its consumer, is not scheduled again with that objective. A frozen module's waves that are
`todo` are re-planned like any other, within its frozen decomposition, and waves may be
appended to it, such as those a module added after it calls for. A change of the
settings' `campaign` answer unfreezes every module, as `modules-schema`'s
Status section describes, and every `todo` wave is re-planned under the new kind.

## 6. Derived paths

A batch's id, `wave-<index>/batch-<index>`, names its branch and worktree, and its wave
index the wave branch, as `versioning` spells them, and with its module its run dirs and
reviews dir, as `layout` spells them, each run's `task.json` naming the batch's wave and
index.

# dependencies.json schema

Field meaning for `<workdir>/crustify/artifacts/dependencies.json`, the out-of-tree
libraries the campaign's target uses. Layout example:
[`templates/dependencies.json`](../../../templates/dependencies.json).

Planning emits it beside `modules.json`, whose dependency records name each library and
count what each module consumes from it; this artifact records each library once, with
the crates assessed for it and every entity the campaign uses of it, mapped to what those
crates offer. How a campaign reaches these libraries is
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md).

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | the analyzed tree's revision, as `modules.json`'s |
| `libraries` | one entry per out-of-tree library a module of `modules.json` depends on |

## 1. libraries[*]

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | the library as linked, such as `libz`; the dependency records' `library` |
| `resolved` | what the target's build found: `path`, the file it linked; `version`, the release, as the build system reports it or the library's version header gives it; and `package`, the system package that installed it, or `null` for a library built from source |
| `source` | the side campaign's `c/`: `repository`, the library's upstream repository, and `tag`, the release `resolved.version` names; and `patches`, the distribution patches to that release, named by the package that carries them, or `null` when there are none |
| `linked_from` | `side-campaign` when the target links the side campaign's per-variant install, `system` when it keeps linking the system's copy, as libc does |
| `candidates` | the crates assessed for it, below; empty when none was found |
| `c_entities` | every entity of the library the campaign uses, each mapped to what the candidates offer for it, below |
| `recommendation` | the plan's route for the library, shaped as `decision` |
| `decision` | how the campaign reaches the library, as the user chose it once the plan was complete, below; `null` until the user decides |
| `crustify_campaign` | the library's side campaign, the crustify campaign the `crustify-campaign` route reaches it through: `repository`, its `crustify-rs/<source>-crustify`, shared by the libraries one source builds, and `pin`, the commit of its working branch the campaign's workspace pins, or `null` until it pins one; `null` when no entity takes that route |

The assessment fields, `resolved`, `source`, `candidates`, `c_entities` but for each
entity's `confirmation`, and `recommendation`, are the plan's; the `decision` is the
user's; and the `crustify_campaign.pin`, each fork's `pin` and each entity's
`confirmation` are progress, recorded as the side campaign, the forks
and the batches advance.

## 2. libraries[*].candidates

The crates that could serve some of what the campaign uses of the library, with the
standard library left out: it is never assessed, and appears only in `c_entities`.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `crate` | the crate's name on crates.io |
| `version` | the version assessed |
| `license` | its SPDX license expression |
| `kind` | `ported` for a crate that reimplements the library in Rust, `bindings` for one that puts a safe Rust API over the C library itself |
| `sys` | for `bindings`, the raw `-sys` crate it builds on, or `null` when it binds the library itself; `null` for `ported` |

[`templates/dependencies.json`](../../../templates/dependencies.json).

Planning emits it beside `modules.json`, whose dependency records name each library and
count what each module consumes from it; this artifact records each library once, with
the crates assessed for it and every entity the campaign uses of it, mapped to what those
crates offer. How a campaign reaches these libraries is
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md).

name = "glibc-bindings"
description = "Safe Rust wrappers over glibc's C API"
version.workspace = true

license.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
repository.workspace = true
publish.workspace = true

[features]
default = ["libc"]

[dependencies]

[dev-dependencies]

trybuild.workspace = true

[lints]
workspace = true

[workspace]
resolver = "3"
members = [".", "libc-sys"]

---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.
