# Binding symbols

How a scheduled C symbol becomes a safe Rust binding: the symbol route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section and reaches the types
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md) binds. [`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md) starts from it.

## 1. Functions

A function is bound as a `pub fn`; it is a `pub unsafe fn` only when no safe type-level
contract can express its caller obligation. Its FFI call, and the raw pointers it
reconstructs for it, sit in its module's `ffi_import` region, as the
[conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions section describes.

Its signature follows the analysis's findings, each argument and return taking the safe
form of what it names:

- **Out-parameters.** A pointer the function only writes through, to hand back a result,
  is part of the return, several of them a tuple, present only in the outcome in which the
  function writes it.
- **Buffers.** A pointer and the count that bounds it are one slice, the count taken from
  it; a buffer the function fills returns the part it filled.
- **Strings.** A NUL-terminated string the function borrows for the call is a borrowed C
  string, or the Rust string or path type of the encoding the analysis establishes,
  converted at the call, an interior NUL rejected before it. A returned string is a borrow
  tied to what keeps it alive, or an owner over its releaser where the caller frees it.
- **Nullability.** A nullable pointer is an `Option`.
- **Errors.** A function that can fail returns a `Result`, its failure read from the error
  convention the analysis establishes: a status return, a sentinel return, or error state
  the library keeps beside the call, read immediately after it, before another call into
  the library can replace it. A return that reports only success is not returned, and an
  outcome its C callers treat as ordinary, such as an exhausted iteration or an absent
  entry, is part of the success value. Each error convention has one error type, carrying
  what the convention reports, `errno`'s being `std::io::Error`.
- **Variadics.** A variadic function is bound through fixed-arity forms: one that formats
  its arguments takes the formatted message, passed to a `"%s"` format, and any other is
  one function per argument list its callers use. A `va_list` function is reached only
  through its variadic sibling.

A `static inline` function a header defines is bound as an exported one is: it is
allowlisted, and called through the raw binding generated for it, as
[`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes. The exception is a short
one whose whole implementation is in the header, which may be ported instead, to save the
cost of an FFI call, unless what it does depends on the build's features or configuration.
A reimplementation is a port, as [`porting`](../../porting/SKILL.md) describes, and is
annotated `Replaces`, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Anchors section describes.

Moved (exclusively or refcounted), borrowed (immutably or mutably), nullable, scalar and
array variants are separate functions when one signature cannot express every valid
contract. A function taking or returning type-erased arguments is generic.

A method is emitted in an `impl T` block on the type it implements, taking `&self` or
`&mut self` as its first argument. A free function stays free.

## 2. Globals

A global is bound as a `'static` borrow, never as an owner, its value taking the safe form
its type takes in a signature, as [Functions](#1-functions) describes. Its access
discipline follows from every C access:

- immutable after initialization: a shared handle;
- synchronized by C: the matching safe synchronization (an atomic, or guards handing out
  the shared or exclusive handle under the lock), never discarding a lock's status;
- otherwise mutable: `unsafe` accessors that exclude concurrent access, reported as such;
- thread-local: a handle borrowed for a closure on the current thread, neither `Send` nor
  `Sync`.

A lock counts only if every access takes it and it rejects same-thread re-entry. A global
C sets up in a routine, rather than in its definition, is reached through the safe API only
once that routine has run, however the binding ensures it.

## 3. Function pointers

A function pointer is bound from its declaration and every site that calls it or supplies
it, a function assigned to it or passed as it. One a typedef declares is named after its
typedef; one written inline is named after the site that declares it, the field,
parameter, return or global, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming
section describes, so that two inline pointers of one signature in one file are two items
when their sites differ.
<!-- TODO: wavefront keys an inline function pointer by its signature and home file, so
the sites of one signature in one file are one item; it has yet to key them by declaring
site, a local's or a cast's folded into the site whose value it carries. -->

It is bound to a safe callable type that holds either of its implementations:

- a Rust closure, which C reaches through a trampoline of the C signature and the context
  C passes back to it; and
- a C function, with its context, which Rust calls: made only inside the crate, through an
  `unsafe` constructor whose contract states what the C that supplies it guarantees, the
  function's validity and its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call, its
  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Three cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type; and
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

  function's validity and its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call, its
  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Three cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type; and
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

## 4. Macros

A C macro is bound to a Rust form of its own:

- a type-generating macro, to one generic type, through [`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md),
  its instances aliases of it;
- a constant macro, to a `const`, defined from its generated binding;
- a symbol alias, through the safe wrapper of the symbol it names, each of whose stand-ins
  stands in for the alias too and carries its anchor beside the symbol's own: where the
  symbol is a lifecycle primitive, the strategy methods that call it, as
  [Lifecycle strategies](#5-lifecycle-strategies) describes; and
- a macro that implements logic, to a function, `#[inline]`, or `const` where its body
  computes on its arguments alone, which reimplements the body and reaches C only for the
  symbols its expansion uses, through their safe wrappers, and for the fields it accesses,
  through their accessors. A `macro_rules!` takes its place only where a function cannot
  express it: control flow that leaves its caller, token pasting or stringification, an
  argument used as a place, or one evaluated lazily or more than once.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration, which the Rust does not see,
is the exception: it is reached through a shim, `crustify_<NAME>`, bound and wrapped.

## 5. Lifecycle strategies

A type's own lifecycle routines are bound with the type, as
[`binding-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section describes. The foundational
modules hold the rest: the allocators or constructors, releasers, disposers and cloners of
type-erased memory and of strings, each with the lifecycle role established while
planning, as [`decomposition`](../../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational
modules section describes. The analysis confirms each role from the item's body, and a role
the body contradicts is corrected, the correction recorded with the batch.

In a foundational module's batch, an item with a lifecycle role becomes a generic policy
or strategy that calls the primitive, through which the owners of strings and of
type-erased singletons and arrays allocate, clone and release what they hold, so that each
owner frees what it holds through the family that allocated it. The primitive itself is
not also exposed as an ordinary safe function. The module's other items follow their
route.

Singleton and array handles have separate policies, each in its primitive's home. A
family's allocator, releaser and cloner form one policy. A releaser that frees a container together with its
elements is no policy of the container: where its body only releases each element and then
the container, the owner holds its elements as their own owners, under the container's
allocator's policy, and releases as the releaser does without calling it; where it does
more, the owner is hand-written.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, the record of what landed and how evolution itself evolves. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

content.content:
---
name: wavefront
description: "Deterministic queries and dependency-ordered plans over the C codebase, the first resort for any question about it: entities, uses, dependencies, pointers, lifecycles, T3 cast tables. Read before querying the C codebase, before planning, decomposing or scheduling, before analysing or binding an item, when packing wrap batches, when reviewing pointer findings or lifecycles, and before changing wavefront itself."
---

# wavefront

Wavefront answers deterministic queries about a C codebase, its entities, their uses and
dependencies, their pointers and lifecycles, and generates dependency-ordered wave plans
over it.

It is the first resort for any question about the C codebase: an entity's definition,
fields or signature, its users, callers and casts, what it depends on, and the pointer
findings and lifecycle roles submitted on it are queried rather than searched for in the
source, so that each answer covers every site the traced build compiles, and every query
of one fact gets one answer. The source is read where wavefront records nothing, to read a
body, and to judge what wavefront records.

Its `README.md` and `--help` are read in full before its first command, and each section
below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. How
wavefront scopes, orders and batches, what its configuration, tables and records hold, and
what each query returns are those documents', and are not restated here. Its goals and
non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to wavefront is judged against, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes.

## Campaign state

Wavefront's repo root is the C root: it is passed `<workdir>/c`, so that every path it
reads and reports is relative to the C root, as the plan records them. Its state sits
under `crustify/wavefront/`, which the configuration names as its `state_dir`,
`../crustify/wavefront`:

- `codeql/`, the CodeQL database and its T1/T2 tables, and `.cache`, both gitignored;
- `configs/wavefront-config.json`, the campaign's configuration, which every query of the
  bindings and reviews resolves through, with `"t3_dir": "t3"`;
- `t3/`, the T3 tables, one campaign-wide pair; and
- `ownership-store.json`, the findings submitted to it through the CLI. A finding
  submitted once is queried again rather than re-derived.

The configuration's `modules` hold one record per module of `modules.json`, named
`<link-unit>/<name>`, with ` (foundational)` after a foundational module's name.

What follows is how wavefront serves each stage: each section names the skill and section
it adds to, and states only what wavefront adds there.

## Setup

### Setup › Provisioning

CodeQL and wavefront's query pack dependencies are installed, as its README describes.
`crustify/.gitignore` lists `wavefront/codeql` and `wavefront/.cache`.

### Setup › Artifact tree

`crustify/wavefront/` is scaffolded for wavefront's state.

### Setup › Baseline

Once the builds and the baseline are recorded, the CodeQL database is created from a
traced build of the `plain` configuration in a fresh scratch dir, with `c/` as its source
root, and its T1/T2 tables are extracted, through a bootstrap configuration in
`crustify/tmp/`; the campaign's own configuration is the plan's.

## Planning

Planning reads `docs/scoping.md`, `docs/graph.md`, `docs/batching.md`,
`docs/type-lifecycle.md`, `docs/artifacts/t3.md` and `docs/artifacts/schedule.md`.

### Decomposition › Runs

Each planner run brings the configuration and the T3 tables up to date with the plan: it
emits what is missing, migrates what follows an earlier wavefront schema, adds what the
scope adds and corrects what is wrong. A changed configuration or T3 row changes the graph,
so the `todo` waves whose batches it moves are re-planned, and the `depends_on` in
`modules.json` when it moves them.

### Decomposition › Dependencies

The configuration's `modules` are authored from `modules.json`: each module's files, with
the entities its `items` list select, each by the kind it is in C. Wavefront refuses an
entry that claims what its file only declares, and a unit two modules claim, so that every
entity is owned by exactly one module; the configuration is verified against the CLI.
<!-- TODO: wavefront makes a unit of every macro an installed header defines, but of an
internal header's macro only where the closure's code expands it, so an internal API macro
no C of the closure expands is planned nowhere, and it makes units of the configuration and
attribute macros the closure expands too. It has yet to make units of the macros that are
API, and only those, count enums and
macros in the modules' records, and tell a closed enum from a flags one, which the planner
judges until then, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes. -->

A module's dependency records are counted from a schedule of the whole closure, without
`schedule_seeds`: its module record's `depends_on` gives its in-tree records, with their
`unique_edges` and `total_edges`; its items give the `counters`, and their references
whose `scope` is `external` the out-of-tree records.

### Decomposition › Foundational modules

The foundational modules' candidates are selected from the configuration's graph, after
the T3 tables are written, so that their cast edges resolve type-erased values: the
type-erased units that no cast edge ties to a named type, and the units whose pointers
carry the `string` property, that depend on no other module's types. Each candidate's body
is read before it is admitted. Each member's lifecycle role is identified as
`docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes and submitted to the ownership store, so that the bindings of
the foundational modules find it.

### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional
  compilation hides from the traced build.

A row wavefront warns is stale is corrected or deleted.

### Scheduling › Waves and batches

- A planner run schedules once, its `schedule_seeds` the files
  of the modules it plans, without batch caps: the waves' batches are packed when each
  starts. The output is written to `crustify/tmp/`, never over `schedule.json`.
- A wrap campaign schedules over the API headers alone, in wavefront's API mode.
- A unit wavefront warns belongs to no module, and a module it warns claims no unit, are
  gaps in the decomposition, corrected before the schedule is used.
- Wavefront's `modules` become `schedule.json`'s, each named back to its `link_unit`,
  `module` and `foundational`, with its `layer`, its waves and its dependency records. Its
  `depends_on.external` records group its units' references whose `scope` is `external`
  by the library whose installed headers define the referenced entity, as
  `dependencies.json` names it; the external entity's own dependencies, which wavefront
  walks too, are the side campaign's to schedule.
- Wavefront numbers its waves from 0 in every run, so the `todo` waves are numbered after
  the highest index of a started wave, in wavefront's order, their `depends_on`
  renumbered. A wave's `items` are those of its wavefront batches, with their `home`, their
  `objective`, their `used_fields` as `field_users`, a macro's `type_generator_for`
  deciding its route, and their release points. An item a started wave holds, or that a

content.content:
# Scoping

A config names the program Wavefront analyzes, its `closure`, and what
`wavefront schedule` orders, its `schedule_seeds`. From the closure Wavefront
composes, in memory, an inventory with two sections and one view; nothing is
written to disk. Field meaning of the config itself is in the
[README](../README.md#configuration).

## Files

`closure.impl_files` names the sources and private headers that implement the
program, and `closure.api_headers` the headers that publish it, each as two
lists: `included` names files and directories, and the optional `excluded`
removes what they would otherwise select. An entry ending in `/` expands to
every C or C++ source and header beneath it, in either list; a file an
`included` entry selects is removed when it matches its key's `excluded` list.
The resulting candidates are then anchored on the T1 tables: a file the traced
build never compiled, or whose body an `#ifdef` elides, contributes no
entities.

The closure is the whole program: the graph, every query and the usage counts
of a schedule's items ([`artifacts/schedule.md`](artifacts/schedule.md#statistics))
read it, whatever part of it a schedule covers. Code the closure leaves out,
such as a test suite, is no use of the program's entities.

## Modules

A module is a named group of the closure's files and of the items they
define, which a schedule orders together: typically a translation unit with
the headers that carry its name, but a group may hold a part of a TU, a
header alone, or several TUs, as its config says. It is unrelated to C++20
modules.

`modules`, optional, groups the closure's units for `wavefront schedule`
([`batching.md`](batching.md#order)). It lists module records,
`{"name": ..., "files": [...]}`: a unique name and file entries, each as
[`schedule_seeds`](#schedule-seeds) writes one. A module claims the units
whose home is one of its files, its defining file or, without one, its
declaration, as its items narrow them. A shared header is split this way,
each module naming the items it defines that the module takes, and a TU
between two modules, one `included` and the other `excluded` the same items.
An item names an entity its file is home to: one its file only declares, its
definition elsewhere, is an error, since the module would not claim it. A
unit two modules claim is an error, and a module that claims no unit of the
closure is warned of. `modules` may cover only part of the closure: the
modules of what a schedule holds, its seeds and every unit they depend on. A
unit the schedule holds that no module claims is ordered alone, and warned
of; one it does not reach needs no module.

## Schedule seeds

`schedule_seeds`, optional, names the units `wavefront schedule` starts from
([`batching.md`](batching.md)). It lists file entries, each a path, a
directory written with a trailing slash, or
`{"path": ..., "items": {"included": [...], "excluded": [...]}}`. A file
seeds the units ([`batching.md`](batching.md#units)) it defines or declares:
`src/libgit2/repository.c` the functions it defines, and
`include/git2/repository.h` those it declares, wherever they are defined. A
schedule holds its seeds and every unit they depend on, so that it is complete
on its own. A config without `schedule_seeds` seeds every unit.

Each item is `{"name": ..., "kind": ...}`, an entity its file defines or
declares: its name, and its kind, what it is in C: `function`, `global`,
`macro`, `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `function_pointer` or `typedef`. A
typedef folds into the struct, union, enum or function pointer it names, and
is a `typedef` only when it names none ([`graph.md`](graph.md#nodes)); a
function pointer written inline is named by its signature. C keeps tags apart from ordinary identifiers, so a struct and a
function or global may share a name in one file, as `static const struct
typelen {...} typelen[]` does; the kind tells them apart. `included` seeds
only the entities it names of its file, `excluded` none of those it names; an
item that names no such entity, gives it a kind it is not, or that both lists
name, is an error, as is a file outside the closure. A directory names the closure's files under it, and takes no items;
one that holds none is an error.

The seeds never change the order: a schedule orders every unit of the
closure and keeps the ones it holds in it, so that schedules of several seeds
are parts of one order, and the selections a consumer makes, by file, module
or any other grouping, of a schedule are too. Two schedules hold
the dependencies they share both; each item's key tells them apart.

## Closure

The **closure** section holds every entity whose definition sits in
`impl_files` or `api_headers`: it says where an entity lives, and nothing
more. An entity with no definition in the database is in it when all of its
declarations sit in those files; a forward declaration of a tag defined
elsewhere is no such entity, and follows its definition, so a closure
header's `struct tm;` leaves the system's `tm` external. A typedef takes the
section of the type it finally names, so a typedef and its struct never fall
on opposite sides. A macro is in the section when a closure file defines it,
a header as much as a `.c` file.

The closure **owns** the entities that are its own to translate: all of the
section but the macros a header defines ([Default mode](#default-mode)). The
default graph walks their bodies, and a header macro's too, and a schedule's
units are drawn from them ([`batching.md`](batching.md#units)).

## External

The **external** section is derived: everything the closure's entities reach
that is defined outside it, its external frontier. Two walks build it:

- **symbols**: from each function the closure owns, through its callees and
  the types its signature and body name; a reached function defined outside
  the closure is external, and is not walked further;
- **types**: through the field graph. A struct of the closure is walked
  through every field; an external one only through the fields the closure's
  code accesses. This pulls in a type embedded by value (`pthread_mutex_t`).

An external item's declaring headers are narrowed to those the closure's
translation unit that reached it actually includes, through the build's
include graph. An item imported through more than one header is marked
`reexport`.

## API view

The **api** view is what `api_headers` publish: every entity declared there,
or defined there outright (an inline function, a macro, a struct with its
layout). It is not a section. Publication and location are independent, so
an entity is in the view and in whichever section holds it: a function an
`api_headers` file declares but that some other library defines is api and
external at once, which is what a re-export is. A header's include guard is
defined there but publishes nothing, and is not in the view.

## Default mode

The default graph and schedule are body-deep:

- a function or global of the closure, or a macro a closure file defines,
  a header's included, depends on what its body calls and touches, a
  macro's body being its replacement list
  ([`graph.md`](graph.md#edges)); an external function contributes its
  signature only, and an external macro nothing;
- a macro a closure header defines is in the closure section but not owned:
  any C still built may include that header, and a `#define` cannot be
  re-exported from Rust, so the macro stays C's, read from its header. Only
  a macro local to a closure translation unit has no other user, and is the
  closure's own. A header macro still has its body edges: one that
  implements logic is rewritten in Rust over what it expands to. A header
  macro is a node when the closure expands it, when it mints a type the
  closure reaches, or when an `api_headers` file defines it: a public macro
  is part of the API whether or not the library's own code expands it;
- a struct defined in a closure file keeps every field edge; an external
  struct only the fields the closure's code accesses;
- a schedule orders every node the closure owns; an external node is a
  dependency of the units that reach it, never a unit.

## API mode

`--api-headers-only` reads the library as its public interface:

- every function contributes its signature only, in the closure or not;
- only a struct the `api_headers` define keeps its field edges; any other
  is an opaque handle;
- only a generator macro the `api_headers` define mints instances: one
  defined elsewhere orders no API type;
- the **API reach** is what the public signatures and fields reach from
  the api view, walked before any cast edge exists. Cast edges are added
  only between its nodes ([`graph.md`](graph.md#type-erasure)), so a cast
  never pulls a type into the reach;
- a schedule seeds only from the api view, and holds what those seeds reach
  of the nodes the closure owns. An external item is a node of the
  graph and a dependency of the items that reach it, but not a unit.
  `query dag --name X --external-only` lists X's external dependencies.

A library is scheduled from a config whose closure covers it, so that the
relations between its parts, cast edges included, are in the one graph its
schedules order them on; a [`schedule_seeds`](#schedule-seeds) selects the part each one
holds.

## Queries

`--closure-only`, `--external-only` and `--api-only` filter `query` output by
section and view. They intersect: `--api-only --external-only` keeps
re-exports. `query files` lists each set's files.
# Batching

`wavefront schedule` orders the units of a config's closure and keeps those
its `schedule_seeds` names, with what they depend on, in waves of batches. It
reads the dependency graph of the closure ([`graph.md`](graph.md)) and its seeds
([`scoping.md`](scoping.md#schedule-seeds)); field meaning of the output is in
[`artifacts/schedule.md`](artifacts/schedule.md).

## Units

The units are every node the closure owns
([`scoping.md`](scoping.md#closure)), its enums included, and every macro the
closure's files define and the graph holds, a header's included: a header
macro is not owned, since C still built may include it, but its Rust
counterpart is still to be written. The graph holds a header macro the closure
expands, one that mints a type the closure reaches, and every one an
`api_headers` file defines but its include guard
([`scoping.md`](scoping.md#default-mode)); a header macro nothing expands and
no header publishes is no unit.
With `--api-headers-only`, they are the owned nodes the api view
publishes, closed over the public-signature graph: a private type a public
signature names is a unit too, as is a macro it reaches. External nodes are
never units; they stay dependencies of the units that reach them.

## Order

The units are ordered over all of them, whatever the seeds, in groups: each
module's ([`scoping.md`](scoping.md#modules)), and each unit no module claims
alone, so that without `modules` every unit is a group of its own. An edge
between two groups weighs the distinct units the one depends on in the other:
a cut leaves each of them to a binding, however many edges reach it. A unit
edge weighs 1 ([`graph.md`](graph.md#cycles)). The groups' cycles are cut as the graph's
are: within each, the group the others depend on most, net of what it depends
on, comes first, and every edge from a group to one placed after it is cut.
The groups are layered by longest path: a module's `layer` is its place in
the order of the modules. Each module's units are then ordered within it,
their own cycles cut the same way, and layered by longest path.

Every unit edge a cut removes, between groups or within a module, stays
recorded on both ends: the user lists the dependency, ordered after it, in its
`depends_on.cut`, and the dependency lists the user, ordered before it, in its
`depended_on_by.cut`. A cut between two modules is recorded on the user's module with
the unit edges it crosses: what the module uses of a module ordered after it.

The schedule keeps the seeds and every unit they depend on, transitively, the
cut dependencies included: a cycle partner is still needed, after its user.
`seeded` tells the seeds from what came along. A schedule of the whole
closure and a narrow one agree on every unit's order and cuts, so that the
schedules of several seeds are parts of one order, and so is any grouping a
consumer makes of a schedule's items by their `defined_in` and `declared_in`.

## Waves

Each layer of a module's units is a wave, its `sublayer` its place among the
module's waves, from 0. A wave depends on its module's previous wave and on
the waves that hold its units' dependencies, the cut ones aside: a consumer
that runs each wave once those complete runs every wave as early as it can,
and one that runs the waves in their listed order, by layer and sublayer,
runs them correctly too, if later.

A unit no module claims, which the schedule warns of, is placed by what it
is:

- a dependency goes in the wave listed right before the first one that
  needs it, so that it arrives when it is needed. Before a module's wave,
  that is the module's previous wave, or a new wave of the module ahead of
  its first, so that the module's waves hold what it needs and its
  `sublayer`s count them all; the item itself still names no module. Before
  a wave with no module, it is a wave of its own;
- a seed keeps its place in the order, in a wave of its own listed before
  the module waves of its layer.

A wave with no module records the `layer` it is listed in. Without
`modules`, no unit is claimed and none is warned of: every wave has no
module, its `layer` its place in the units' order, and a dependency goes in
the previous layer's wave.

## Batches

Without caps, a wave holds two batches: one of its structs, unions, enums
and generator macros, then one of its functions, globals, other macros,
function pointers and typedefs. Its consumer splits them by the items' statistics
([`artifacts/schedule.md`](artifacts/schedule.md#items)).

Any cap packs each wave into batches, in name order, and lets a module's
adjacent layers of units fold into one wave while their merged units still pack into a
single batch: one user then receives them in layer order, so a producer
still comes before its consumer. A fold never creates two batches, which
would run in parallel. A cap that is not given bounds nothing.

**Type batches** close before a type is added when they already hold
`--max-types` types, when the declared fields they hold reach `--min-fields`,
or when the new type alone has `--min-fields` fields or more. A wide type
therefore gets a batch of its own. A type batch's `source_file` is its first
type's defining file.

**Symbol batches** close before a symbol is added when they already hold
`--max-syms` symbols, or when the symbol's body LoC would take their total
past `--max-loc`. A symbol longer than `--max-loc` alone gets a batch of its
own; `--max-loc 0` disables the LoC cap.

| flag | bounds |
|---|---|
| `--max-types` | types in a type batch |
| `--min-fields` | declared fields that close a type batch, and isolate a wide type |
| `--max-syms` | symbols in a symbol batch |
| `--max-loc` | summed body LoC in a symbol batch |

The schedule records the caps under `caps`, `null` for each one not given.

## Used fields

Each type unit carries the fields its users reach (`used_fields`). An API
schedule lists every field of a type the `api_headers` define, and none of a
type defined elsewhere, whose layout the API does not publish. A default
schedule lists the fields the config's own functions access.

## Release points

A unit's users are processed in the order too, and each one's place tells a
consumer when the unit is no longer needed in its original form:

- a struct, union or enum is **opaque** after its **layout users**: the
  functions, globals and aggregates that read its members, name an enum's
  enumerators, take its size, alignment or an offset into it, hold it by
  value, or step a pointer over it (`t2/layout_uses.csv`). Once all of them
  are processed, what remains holds it only through pointers. A type held by
  value inside another is also used by every layout user of its holder,
  transitively, since they depend on the holder's layout and so on its own.
  An enum is used whole wherever it is used at all, so once it is opaque C
  holds it, if at all, only through a pointer;
- a struct or union's memory is **unmanaged** after its **raw sites**: the functions
  that allocate it with an allocator of untyped memory, or free or dispose
  of it with a releaser of untyped memory. Once all of them are processed,
  no C hands its storage to C's allocator, and a consumer may move it to
  another. Its own constructors, destructors and cloners are functions like
  any other, unreferenced after their callers: what they call does not
  matter to C, which only calls them;
- a function, global, macro, function pointer or typedef is
  **unreferenced** after its **referrers**: the units that call it, take its
  address, access it, expand it or name it, the edges of the body-deep graph
  into it, a macro's replacement list among them
  ([`graph.md`](graph.md#edges)). A macro's referrers are the functions
  whose bodies expand it, through another macro's expansion too, the macros
  whose replacement lists do, and the types whose declarations do
  (`char buf[GIT_OID_MAX_SIZE]`). A function pointer a typedef declares is
  referred to by what names the typedef or an alias of it, and by the code
  that calls through it;
- a function pointer written inline has no name, so C needs its signature
  for as long as anything reaches a **site** that writes it
  (`t2/function_pointer_uses.csv`, a row per site, naming the signature, the
  file it is homed in and the entity that writes it). Its users are each site
  and what reaches the site from outside:

  | site | reached by |
  |---|---|
  | a struct's field | the struct's layout users: `s->open(...)` reads the field |
  | a function's parameter or return | the function's referrers, which pass or receive it |
  | a global | the global's referrers |
  | a function's local, or a cast in it | nothing: only the function sees it |

  One signature written at several sites of its file is one function
  pointer, and has the users of every site.

Users are read off the body-deep graph, the layout-use table and, for raw
sites, `t2/arg_casts.csv`. Only the closure's units count: an external
function or a test the closure leaves out is no user. A macro is no layout
user either, since its uses are recorded where it is expanded.

A schedule made with `--api-headers-only` has no release points: its items'
`opaque_after`, `memory_unmanaged_after` and `unreferenced_after` are `null`. It binds what the
headers publish and keeps the C behind it, so nothing it schedules retires a
layout or an export, and its order, the API graph's, does not hold most of
the users.

Each item records its release points, `opaque_after` and `memory_unmanaged_after`
or `unreferenced_after`
([`artifacts/schedule.md`](artifacts/schedule.md#release-points)); their
users are a query away, `query structs --layout-users`, `query structs
--raw-sites` and `query functions --callers`.
The point is a frontier rather than one wave: the waves are listed in one
topological order, which puts a wave after others it does not depend on, so
the point is, of the unit's own wave and its scheduled users', those no other
one depends on, transitively through `depends_on.scheduled`. Its items are the users in
those waves, the unit itself when its own wave is one: within a wave nothing
is ordered, so each of them is a last user. A consumer that runs waves once
their dependencies complete has released the unit once all of them have; one
that runs them in their listed order, once the highest has. The modules
answer the same over the order of the modules, counting a user no module
claims toward the module whose wave holds it: a consumer that switches a
module whole, once its last wave has run, reads them rather than the waves,
since a user's wave can end before the module that holds it does.

Each point has two records, `closure` over every user and `scheduled` over
those the schedule holds. A narrow schedule may leave users out: a user
depends on the unit, not the other way round, so the unit's seeds need not
reach it. Its `scheduled` record then counts fewer users, and its waves are a
lower bound, while the `closure` record names the last users in the order of
the whole closure, which a narrow schedule keeps, and their modules.

The layout uses are syntactic, as every fact is
([`graph.md`](graph.md#assumptions-and-limitations)): a size written as a
number, or an offset computed by hand, reads no layout Wavefront can see, and
neither does a byte buffer copied without `sizeof` of the type, or a union
that puns it.

### Raw sites

The raw routines are the ownership store's: a lifecycle role on a
type-erased pointer ([`type-lifecycle.md`](type-lifecycle.md)), a dropper,
a disposer or an out-parameter allocator acting on its `void *` parameter,
an allocator or a deep cloner returning new untyped storage. They are the
`void` lifecycle, established while planning; a store without them knows no
raw site, and `memory_unmanaged_after` is `null`. A role on a typed pointer is no
raw routine, whatever it calls.

A raw site is one conversion `t2/arg_casts.csv` records at a raw routine's
parameter or return, and its type is what the conversion's other end holds,
nothing being followed further:

| the other end | the type |
|---|---|
| a value of a named type: `free(db)`, `db = malloc(...)` | that type |
| a slot declared to hold one: a typed parameter, field or return | that type |
| a `void *` parameter | the one type its body reads it as, or what T3 `erased_arg` rows say it holds. A parameter read as several types is dispatched on (`opt_free_elem(type, void *ptr)`), and its free is one branch's: it names none |
| a `void *` field | every type stored into it or read out of it, less T3 `drop` rows, with T3 `erased_field` rows: freeing the field frees whatever any instance stored (`av_freep(&ctx->priv_data)`) |
| a scalar pointer: a byte or character buffer | none: it holds no struct |

A raw site on a type-erased end that names no type is unresolved: a byte
buffer in a `void *` field, a raw routine wrapping another, a generic
container's storage. A schedule warns of how many there are, and
`query structs --raw-sites --unresolved` lists them; T3 rows type those that
hold a struct. A named type's conversion carries no pointer depth, so the
storage of a `T **` array of pointers counts as `T`'s, which errs late.

# Scoping

A config names the program Wavefront analyzes, its `closure`, and what
`wavefront schedule` orders, its `schedule_seeds`. From the closure Wavefront
composes, in memory, an inventory with two sections and one view; nothing is
written to disk. Field meaning of the config itself is in the
[README](../README.md#configuration).

## Files

`closure.impl_files` names the sources and private headers that implement the
program, and `closure.api_headers` the headers that publish it, each as two
lists: `included` names files and directories, and the optional `excluded`
removes what they would otherwise select. An entry ending in `/` expands to
every C or C++ source and header beneath it, in either list; a file an
`included` entry selects is removed when it matches its key's `excluded` list.
The resulting candidates are then anchored on the T1 tables: a file the traced
build never compiled, or whose body an `#ifdef` elides, contributes no
entities.

The closure is the whole program: the graph, every query and the usage counts
of a schedule's items ([`artifacts/schedule.md`](artifacts/schedule.md#statistics))
read it, whatever part of it a schedule covers. Code the closure leaves out,
such as a test suite, is no use of the program's entities.

## Modules

A module is a named group of the closure's files and of the items they
define, which a schedule orders together: typically a translation unit with
the headers that carry its name, but a group may hold a part of a TU, a
header alone, or several TUs, as its config says. It is unrelated to C++20
modules.

`modules`, optional, groups the closure's units for `wavefront schedule`
([`batching.md`](batching.md#order)). It lists module records,
`{"name": ..., "files": [...]}`: a unique name and file entries, each as
[`schedule_seeds`](#schedule-seeds) writes one. A module claims the units
whose home is one of its files, its defining file or, without one, its
declaration, as its items narrow them. A shared header is split this way,
each module naming the items it defines that the module takes, and a TU
between two modules, one `included` and the other `excluded` the same items.
An item names an entity its file is home to: one its file only declares, its
definition elsewhere, is an error, since the module would not claim it. A
unit two modules claim is an error, and a module that claims no unit of the
closure is warned of. `modules` may cover only part of the closure: the
modules of what a schedule holds, its seeds and every unit they depend on. A
unit the schedule holds that no module claims is ordered alone, and warned
of; one it does not reach needs no module.

## Schedule seeds

`schedule_seeds`, optional, names the units `wavefront schedule` starts from
([`batching.md`](batching.md)). It lists file entries, each a path, a
directory written with a trailing slash, or
`{"path": ..., "items": {"included": [...], "excluded": [...]}}`. A file
seeds the units ([`batching.md`](batching.md#units)) it defines or declares:
`src/libgit2/repository.c` the functions it defines, and
`include/git2/repository.h` those it declares, wherever they are defined. A
schedule holds its seeds and every unit they depend on, so that it is complete
on its own. A config without `schedule_seeds` seeds every unit.

Each item is `{"name": ..., "kind": ...}`, an entity its file defines or
declares: its name, and its kind, what it is in C: `function`, `global`,
`macro`, `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `function_pointer` or `typedef`. A
typedef folds into the struct, union, enum or function pointer it names, and
is a `typedef` only when it names none ([`graph.md`](graph.md#nodes)); a
function pointer written inline is named by its signature. C keeps tags apart from ordinary identifiers, so a struct and a
function or global may share a name in one file, as `static const struct
typelen {...} typelen[]` does; the kind tells them apart. `included` seeds
only the entities it names of its file, `excluded` none of those it names; an
item that names no such entity, gives it a kind it is not, or that both lists
name, is an error, as is a file outside the closure. A directory names the closure's files under it, and takes no items;
one that holds none is an error.

The seeds never change the order: a schedule orders every unit of the
closure and keeps the ones it holds in it, so that schedules of several seeds
are parts of one order, and the selections a consumer makes, by file, module
or any other grouping, of a schedule are too. Two schedules hold
the dependencies they share both; each item's key tells them apart.

## Closure

The **closure** section holds every entity whose definition sits in
`impl_files` or `api_headers`: it says where an entity lives, and nothing
more. An entity with no definition in the database is in it when all of its
declarations sit in those files; a forward declaration of a tag defined
elsewhere is no such entity, and follows its definition, so a closure

section of the type it finally names, so a typedef and its struct never fall
